screens.title: Managing IaC State, Rollbacks, and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on the operational side of Infrastructure as Code — the state CloudFormation tracks, how automatic rollbacks protect you, and how to diagnose failures so you can recover reliably. You will learn why CloudFormation’s declarative model matters: you declare the desired state, CloudFormation holds the internal record and takes the actions needed to reach that state. We’ll also walk through the most common failure modes, how to read CloudFormation Events for actionable errors, and when you must intervene manually for a ROLLBACK_FAILED stack. You will see practical protections such as DeletionPolicy and Stack Termination Protection that prevent accidental data loss, and we’ll reinforce best practices for idempotent custom resources and minimal deployment roles. By the end, you’ll understand not just how to deploy infrastructure, but how to keep it healthy and recoverable — a critical skill for running production systems safely.

Managing IaC State, Rollbacks, and Troubleshooting

Learn how CloudFormation tracks the desired state, how automatic rollbacks protect stacks, and the practical steps to diagnose and recover from failed deployments. We emphasize safe protections and idempotent custom resource design.

screens.title: Declarative IaC: Desired State and Stack State
screens.narratorSegment: Declarative IaC means you describe the desired state of your infrastructure and let the platform determine the exact actions needed to reach that state. In CloudFormation the service keeps an internal record of the stack: which resources it created, their logical and physical IDs, and their current status. Unlike tools that maintain an external editable state file, CloudFormation’s state is internal and authoritative. For CDK, your application code is synthesized into a CloudFormation template and then CloudFormation assumes responsibility for tracking state. This matters because you do not script the sequence of A P I calls; you express the end goal, and CloudFormation resolves dependencies, creates or updates resources, and can roll changes back if something fails. A common misconception is that you can edit CloudFormation’s internal state as a file; you cannot. If resources drift because someone changed them manually outside CloudFormation, future updates may fail or behave unexpectedly. For example, if a database engine parameter was altered by hand, an update that expects the previous value could fail to apply. The practical takeaway is to treat CloudFormation as the single source of truth for resources it manages, and to use CDK only to generate templates that CloudFormation will operate on. How might you enforce that discipline in a team? Make CloudFormation the approved path for changes and audit manual changes regularly.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: CloudFormation is declarative and stores stack state internally; CDK synthesizes to CloudFormation so the service remains authoritative.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Declarative IaC
Claim
CloudFormation records the desired and current status of managed resources internally and uses that record to plan create, update, or delete actions.
Why this matters
  • It ensures consistent updates across dependent resources.
  • It prevents you from hand-editing state; manual changes introduce drift.
  • CDK produces templates for CloudFormation, but CloudFormation remains authoritative.
Common misconception
Some teams expect to edit a state file like Terraform; CloudFormation does not expose such a file, so protect resources by using CloudFormation for all changes.
Concrete example
# CDK app synthesizes to CloudFormation template # The template becomes the source CloudFormation compares against its internal state
Check your understanding
If someone modifies a production database outside CloudFormation, what failure might you expect during the next stack update? Think about ROLLBACK_FAILED scenarios and how to discover the drift using Events.
Key Takeaway

Treat CloudFormation stacks as the single source of truth. Use CDK only to generate templates that CloudFormation manages.

screens.title: How CloudFormation Determines Actions
screens.narratorSegment: CloudFormation implements a compare-and-apply process: when you submit a new template, it compares the template’s desired state with the stack’s current internal state and then computes a set of actions to reconcile the two. The possible actions are typically create, update, or delete for individual resources. Dependency relationships are evaluated so resources are changed in a safe order. For example, if a new property requires replacing an instance, CloudFormation will create the replacement resource before deleting the original when safe to do so, or perform an update in-place where supported. A helpful way to think about this is as a planner: you declare the goal, and CloudFormation decides the safe steps. A common misconception is that CloudFormation always replaces resources on any change; in reality it only replaces when the resource type or property requires replacement. To preview these computed actions use a dry-run style approach: for CDK you can run a diff to see what CloudFormation will change; for templates inspect change sets. Knowing the planned actions reduces surprises and gives you a chance to add protections like DeletionPolicy before destructive changes occur. When you see a planned replacement, confirm backups and retention policies are set for critical data stores.

keyIdea.text: CloudFormation compares the desired template to the internal state and computes a plan of create, update, or delete actions that respect resource dependencies.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Compare & Reconcile
Step 1 — Analyze
CloudFormation reads the incoming template and the stack’s internal record to determine the difference.
Step 2 — Plan
It computes a set of actions: create, update, or delete and orders them by dependencies.
Step 3 — Execute
CloudFormation attempts the changes, and will automatically roll back on failure unless otherwise configured.
Practical checks
  • Use CDK diff or change sets to preview replacements.
  • Confirm DeletionPolicy for resources that must not be lost.
  • Back up data before changes that may replace resources.
Example scenario
Changing a property that requires replacement will result in a create followed by delete workflow or an in-place update when supported. Preview changes first to avoid surprises.
Key Takeaway

Preview planned actions and set protection policies before executing updates that could replace critical resources.

screens.title: CDK Deploys and the CloudFormation Handoff
screens.narratorSegment: CDK is a high-level authoring tool that produces CloudFormation templates. When you run a deploy command the CDK synthesizes application code into a template and then kicks off a CloudFormation deployment. Because CloudFormation executes the deployment, troubleshooting follows the same pattern as for raw templates: inspect the CloudFormation Events for failures. A useful habit is to run a preview step—cdk diff—to see what CloudFormation will change; this can catch many configuration errors before you deploy. If a cdk deploy fails, do not stop at the CDK output alone. Open the CloudFormation console for the corresponding stack and read the Events tab. Events present a chronological log of each resource action and will include status reasons for failures, such as missing permissions or invalid parameter values. Remember that the CDK command is a convenience: the runtime authority that maintains state and performs rollbacks is CloudFormation. This means your recovery steps involve CloudFormation actions like continue-update-rollback, manual resource deletion, or stack update once the root cause is corrected. A common misconception is to assume CDK will mask CloudFormation errors; it will not. Treat CDK as a template authoring layer and CloudFormation as the execution engine to debug.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › CDK → CloudFormation
Walkthrough
When you run a CDK deployment it synthesizes a CloudFormation template and triggers a CloudFormation stack change. If deployment fails, open the stack Events to see the detailed status reasons.
Best practice
Use a preview step to view planned changes and catch replacements or destructive actions before they run.
Example — preview
# Run a diff or preview step (visual only)
# Inspect planned changes and replacements before deploying
If a cdk deploy produces a failure, locate the CloudFormation stack and read the Events tab for resource-level error messages and status reasons. Use those messages to identify permission issues, invalid parameters, or failing custom resources.
Pro tip

Always check CloudFormation Events rather than relying only on CDK output; the Events give the resource-level failure reason.

screens.title: Automatic Rollback and ROLLBACK_FAILED
screens.narratorSegment: CloudFormation’s automatic rollback is a safety net: if a stack creation or update fails, CloudFormation attempts to revert the stack to the previous stable state so you don’t end up with partially applied infrastructure. This behavior prevents inconsistent systems but does not remove the need for operator understanding. Rollbacks can fail, producing a ROLLBACK_FAILED state when CloudFormation cannot revert one or more resources. Typical reasons include manual modifications that introduced drift, custom resource delete handlers that return errors, or dependencies that block deletion. When that happens you must intervene: examine the Events log to identify the failing resource, inspect resource-specific logs such as CloudWatch Logs for custom Lambdas, and decide whether to manually revert the resource, delete it, or skip its rollback and continue using CloudFormation’s CLI options to target resources to skip. A common mistake is to immediately delete the stack when ROLLBACK_FAILED appears. Deleting the stack without understanding the retention policies can lead to data loss. Instead, identify the resource at fault, correct the underlying issue or use targeted operations to reach a stable state, and then re-run the update or delete. The best practice is to have DeletionPolicy configured for critical resources so a failed rollback does not result in unexpected data removal.

keyIdea.title: Rollback behavior
keyIdea.text: Automatic rollback aims to restore the previous stable state; a ROLLBACK_FAILED requires manual diagnosis of the problematic resource and careful recovery steps.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Rollback & Failures
Automatic rollback
On failure CloudFormation attempts to revert all changes to bring the stack back to its previous stable state. This helps avoid partially applied deployments.
When rollbacks fail
  • Manual drift causes inability to revert a resource.
  • Custom resource delete logic fails or returns error.
  • Inter-resource dependencies prevent deletion.
Recovery steps
  1. Open the stack Events and find the FAILED event and its status reason.
  2. Inspect resource-specific logs, for example CloudWatch for custom Lambdas.
  3. Manually fix or delete the problematic resource, or use the CLI to skip its rollback if safe.
Common mistake

Deleting the stack immediately can cause data loss if DeletionPolicy was not set. Diagnose first and recover the resource where possible.

screens.title: Troubleshooting with CloudFormation Events
screens.narratorSegment: The primary troubleshooting tool for a failing CloudFormation deployment is the Events tab on the stack. Events present a chronological record of each action CloudFormation attempted and its outcome, including resource logical ID, action type, status, and a status reason when an error occurs. When you see a FAILED event, read the provided status reason: it commonly identifies an access-denied problem, an invalid parameter, or a resource creation failure. For custom resources the status reason may point to the custom Lambda failing; in that case, switch to the Lambda’s CloudWatch Logs. When diagnosing, take a methodical approach: first identify the earliest FAILED event in the timeline, then follow any dependent resource failures that cascade after that. Don’t assume the last event is the root cause. Also check whether the stack ended in ROLLBACK_COMPLETE or ROLLBACK_FAILED. If ROLLBACK_FAILED appears, the Events will tell you which resource could not be reverted, which is the place to start manual recovery. A misconception is to rely solely on the top-level CLI error; often the Events contain the precise resource-level detail you need to fix the problem. Use Events, then resource logs, then configuration or IAM fixes to resolve the root cause.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Start with the CloudFormation Events timeline to find the first FAILED event, then inspect resource logs and permissions to resolve the root cause.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Events-driven diagnosis
What to look for
  • Find the earliest FAILED event in the timeline.
  • Read the Status reason field for a resource-level error message.
  • Note whether the stack moved to ROLLBACK_COMPLETE or ROLLBACK_FAILED.
Common status reasons
  • Resource creation failed — check resource properties.
  • Access Denied — review deployment role permissions.
  • Invalid parameter value — validate inputs such as AMI IDs or CIDR blocks.
Event sample: RESOURCE_FAILED - Status reason: Access Denied
Recovery checklist
Identify the failing resource, inspect resource logs (for Lambdas check CloudWatch), fix permissions or parameters, and then re-deploy the corrected template. If rollback failed, plan manual intervention for the problematic resource before continuing.

screens.title: Custom Resources: Idempotency and Error Handling
screens.narratorSegment: Custom resources extend CloudFormation with logic you implement, commonly in Lambda functions. Because CloudFormation may call create, update, and delete handlers multiple times, your handlers must be idempotent: running them more than once should result in the same end state as running them once. Implement idempotency by detecting existing resources or using stable identifiers so repeated calls do not create duplicates. For error handling, ensure your function catches exceptions and sends a clear FAILED signal back to CloudFormation with a helpful status reason. Logs are critical: if a custom resource fails, the Lambda’s CloudWatch Logs will contain stack traces and contextual details. A common error is missing try-except blocks or failing to handle timeout conditions, which prevents CloudFormation from receiving a proper failure response and can lead to rollback problems. Remember that CloudFormation will attempt to delete a resource during rollback; ensure your delete handler can handle partial state or missing dependencies gracefully. Treat custom resource development like A P I design: provide clear failure messages, handle retries safely, and document the expected lifecycle so debugging is straightforward when an error appears in Events.

keyIdea.title: Custom resources

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Custom Resource Safety
Idempotency rules
  • Detect existing resources and avoid duplicate creation.
  • Use stable identifiers so repeated calls converge to the same state.
  • Make delete handlers tolerant of partial or missing state.
Error handling
Wrap logic in try-except blocks, log a clear status reason to CloudWatch, and ensure the handler sends a FAILED signal when necessary so CloudFormation receives meaningful feedback.
Concrete scenario
# Lambda create handler must check for existing resource # If resource exists, return success with its identifier # On error, log and return a clear failure reason to CloudFormation
Pro tip

Treat custom resource handlers as durable APIs: predictable, idempotent, and well-logged so rollbacks and retries are safe.

screens.title: Resource DeletionPolicy: Retain, Snapshot, Delete
screens.narratorSegment: DeletionPolicy is an attribute you apply to individual CloudFormation resources to control their behavior when the stack is deleted. There are three common values: Retain, Snapshot, and Delete. Retain ensures the resource persists after the stack is removed, which is useful for S3 buckets that contain critical data you cannot lose. Snapshot is appropriate for resources like RDS databases or EBS volumes where you want CloudFormation to create a final snapshot before deleting; that snapshot provides a recovery point. Delete is the default and allows CloudFormation to remove the resource during stack deletion. Applying DeletionPolicy is a safety decision: for production databases you usually want Snapshot, and for critical storage you often want Retain. A frequent operational error is omitting these settings and later discovering that a delete removed important data. The chapter provides a YAML snippet that shows how to set DeletionPolicy for a resource. Use these attributes thoughtfully and document the rationale in your templates so reviewers understand why a resource is being retained or snapshotted. Resource DeletionPolicy: Retain, Snapshot, Delete means set deletionpolicy to retain or snapshot for critical resources to prevent accidental data loss during stack deletion.. In practical terms, control what happens to resources when stacks are deleted. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DeletionPolicy
keyIdea.text: Set DeletionPolicy to Retain or Snapshot for critical resources to prevent accidental data loss during stack deletion.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › DeletionPolicy
Options explained
  • Retain: keep the resource when the stack is deleted.
  • Snapshot: create a snapshot of the resource before deletion.
  • Delete: remove the resource (default).
When to use each
Use Retain for buckets with critical assets, Snapshot for databases you may need to restore, and Delete for ephemeral infrastructure.
YAML example
Resources:
  MyProductionDatabase:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    DeletionPolicy: Retain # Prevents accidental deletion
    Properties:
      # ...
Verify these settings in your templates before deploying to production so that deletion actions are safe.

screens.title: Stack Termination Protection
screens.narratorSegment: Stack Termination Protection is a stack-level safeguard that prevents accidental deletion of an entire stack. When enabled, attempts to delete the stack will fail until termination protection is explicitly disabled. This is particularly important for production stacks that own critical resources. You can toggle termination protection in the console or via the CLI. The practical sequence is simple: enable protection for production stacks after deployment, and when deletion is intentionally required, explicitly disable it first and then delete. Attempting to delete a protected stack is a safe failure mode that forces the operator to make a conscious decision. A common operational oversight is forgetting to disable protection before scripting a teardown; ensure automation accounts for the required change. Using termination protection together with DeletionPolicy configuration provides a layered approach: termination protection prevents accidental stack deletion, while DeletionPolicy controls what happens to individual resources when a delete is performed intentionally. Think of termination protection as a last-line guard that converts accidental deletions into audible warnings for the operator to resolve deliberately. Stack Termination Protection means enable stack termination protection on production stacks to prevent accidental deletion; disable it deliberately before any intended delete.. In practical terms, enable and disable termination protection to safeguard entire stacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Idempotency and Least-Privilege Deployment Roles
screens.narratorSegment: Idempotency and permission hygiene are two pillars of safe IaC operations. Idempotency ensures that running the same operation multiple times yields the same result; this is especially important for custom resources and deployment scripts that may be retried during rollbacks. Implement idempotency by checking for existing resources, using stable names or identifiers, and writing delete handlers that tolerate partially created state. On the permission side, grant the deployment role only the actions required to provision the resources. Over-permissive roles can cause unintended changes or obscure failure causes. A common error is giving the role broad admin rights to avoid permission errors during testing, which hides the real permissions the template needs and increases blast radius in production. When you face an Access Denied status in Events, tighten the role by adding the minimal missing permissions rather than making the role overly permissive. Together, these practices reduce surprises during updates and make rollbacks and recovery steps more predictable and safe for production environments. Idempotency and Least-Privilege Deployment Roles means make handlers idempotent and deploy with least-privilege roles so retries and rollbacks behave predictably while minimizing risk.. In practical terms, designing safe custom resources and minimal permission sets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Make handlers idempotent and deploy with least-privilege roles so retries and rollbacks behave predictably while minimizing risk.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Simulate Failure and Recover
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on workflow guides you through a controlled failure and recovery. First, deploy the provided critical-app-template with a parameter that forces a failing custom resource. The failure will produce a FAILED event; open the CloudFormation Events tab and read the status reason to identify the ServiceToken or custom resource error. Observe the stack state — it may reach ROLLBACK_COMPLETE or ROLLBACK_FAILED. If it becomes ROLLBACK_FAILED, identify the resource that could not be reverted. Next, modify the template to remove or disable the failing custom resource or set the failure parameter to false and re-run the deployment. After the successful update, enable stack termination protection to secure the stack, then attempt to delete the stack to verify that termination protection blocks deletion. Finally, disable termination protection and delete the stack, then confirm DeletionPolicy behavior: your S3 bucket should remain if Retain was set, and RDS should have a snapshot if Snapshot was set. This lab connects diagnosis in Events to practical recovery actions and demonstrates how DeletionPolicy and termination protection protect data during destructive operations. keyIdea.text: Simulate a controlled failure, read Events to find the cause, fix the template, and verify protections such as Retain and Snapshot during deletion.

Instructor steps (summary)
  1. Deploy the template with the failure parameter enabled to trigger a custom resource error.

screens.title: Common Failure Reasons and Remedies
screens.narratorSegment: When a deployment fails, a few error reasons appear repeatedly and each has a clear remediation path. Resource creation failed often points to misconfigured properties — compare the template properties against the resource documentation and correct invalid values such as wrong AMI IDs or invalid CIDR blocks. Access Denied indicates missing IAM permissions for the deployment role; identify the missing action in the Events and add the minimal permission rather than broadening the role excessively. Invalid parameter value means a parameter passed to the template is out of range or wrong type; validate parameter constraints and defaults and restrict allowed values where possible. Custom resource failures require inspecting the custom Lambda’s CloudWatch Logs to find exception traces, then making handlers idempotent and returning clear failure reasons. A practical remediation workflow is: 1) find the earliest FAILED event in Events, 2) read the status reason, 3) check resource logs if custom, 4) fix the template or permissions, and 5) redeploy. Avoid the trap of treating the last event as root cause — dependencies can cause cascading failures after the initial error. If rollback fails, plan manual remediation for the problematic resource and use the CLI to skip resources during continue-update-rollback only if you understand the consequences.

keyIdea.title: Failure → Remedy
keyIdea.text: Match the Event status reason to a focused fix: configuration, permissions, parameter validation, or custom resource logic, and follow a methodical recovery sequence.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Failures & Remedies
Resource creation failed
Check template resource properties, validate AMI IDs and CIDR blocks, and correct invalid inputs.
Access Denied
Identify missing permissions from Events and add the minimal required IAM actions to the deployment role.
Invalid parameter value
Validate parameter definitions and AllowedValues and correct any incorrect inputs before redeploying.
Custom resource failure
Inspect CloudWatch Logs for the Lambda, make handlers idempotent, and return clear FAILED signals with descriptive reasons.
ROLLBACK_FAILED
Identify the resource that could not be reverted, fix or manually delete it, then continue update rollback or correct and redeploy.
Remediation sequence
Find the earliest FAILED event, read its status reason, check resource logs, apply a focused fix, and redeploy. Avoid deleting the stack prematurely.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on the operational side of Infrastructure as Code — the state CloudFormation tracks, how automatic rollbacks protect you, and how to diagnose failures so you can recover reliably. You will learn why CloudFormation’s declarative model matters: you declare the desired state, CloudFormation holds the internal record and takes the actions needed to reach that state. We’ll also walk through the most common failure modes, how to read CloudFormation Events for actionable errors, and when you must intervene manually for a ROLLBACK_FAILED stack. You will see practical protections such as DeletionPolicy and Stack Termination Protection that prevent accidental data loss, and we’ll reinforce best practices for idempotent custom resources and minimal deployment roles. By the end, you’ll understand not just how to deploy infrastructure, but how to keep it healthy and recoverable — a critical skill for running production systems safely.

By the end of these slides you will have practical operational skills for CloudFormation and CDK deployments. You will be able to explain how CloudFormation stores an internal stack state and why that declarative model means you describe the desired state, not the step-by-step actions. You will also learn how to detect and interpret failed events, including common error reasons such as access denied, invalid parameters, and resource creation failures. A second skill set focuses on protective controls: how to set DeletionPolicy to retain or snapshot critical resources, and how to enable stack termination protection so production stacks cannot be removed accidentally. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic or visual reminder to make retention easier and to link diagnosis to recovery steps you can perform confidently in a real environment.

This second objectives slide expands operational competencies you will practice. First, you will learn to configure and verify DeletionPolicy options: Retain, Snapshot, and Delete, and decide when each is appropriate for production databases and buckets. Second, you will practice enabling and disabling Stack Termination Protection and understanding how it prevents accidental deletion until explicitly removed. Third, we cover idempotency and error handling for custom resources—ensuring create, update, and delete handlers behave reliably and return clear failure signals. Finally, you will master permission hygiene: using minimal deployment permissions to avoid unauthorized actions while still allowing CloudFormation to perform required operations. Each objective connects to hands-on tasks you will perform in the lab so these operational skills become routine parts of your deployment workflow. Learning Objectives — Advanced Operations means protect critical data, design idempotent custom resources, and use least-privilege deployment roles to reduce risk.. In practical terms, skills for resilient iac deployments and safe recoveries. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Declarative IaC means you describe the desired state of your infrastructure and let the platform determine the exact actions needed to reach that state. In CloudFormation the service keeps an internal record of the stack: which resources it created, their logical and physical IDs, and their current status. Unlike tools that maintain an external editable state file, CloudFormation’s state is internal and authoritative. For CDK, your application code is synthesized into a CloudFormation template and then CloudFormation assumes responsibility for tracking state. This matters because you do not script the sequence of A P I calls; you express the end goal, and CloudFormation resolves dependencies, creates or updates resources, and can roll changes back if something fails. A common misconception is that you can edit CloudFormation’s internal state as a file; you cannot. If resources drift because someone changed them manually outside CloudFormation, future updates may fail or behave unexpectedly. For example, if a database engine parameter was altered by hand, an update that expects the previous value could fail to apply. The practical takeaway is to treat CloudFormation as the single source of truth for resources it manages, and to use CDK only to generate templates that CloudFormation will operate on. How might you enforce that discipline in a team? Make CloudFormation the approved path for changes and audit manual changes regularly.

CloudFormation implements a compare-and-apply process: when you submit a new template, it compares the template’s desired state with the stack’s current internal state and then computes a set of actions to reconcile the two. The possible actions are typically create, update, or delete for individual resources. Dependency relationships are evaluated so resources are changed in a safe order. For example, if a new property requires replacing an instance, CloudFormation will create the replacement resource before deleting the original when safe to do so, or perform an update in-place where supported. A helpful way to think about this is as a planner: you declare the goal, and CloudFormation decides the safe steps. A common misconception is that CloudFormation always replaces resources on any change; in reality it only replaces when the resource type or property requires replacement. To preview these computed actions use a dry-run style approach: for CDK you can run a diff to see what CloudFormation will change; for templates inspect change sets. Knowing the planned actions reduces surprises and gives you a chance to add protections like DeletionPolicy before destructive changes occur. When you see a planned replacement, confirm backups and retention policies are set for critical data stores.

CDK is a high-level authoring tool that produces CloudFormation templates. When you run a deploy command the CDK synthesizes application code into a template and then kicks off a CloudFormation deployment. Because CloudFormation executes the deployment, troubleshooting follows the same pattern as for raw templates: inspect the CloudFormation Events for failures. A useful habit is to run a preview step—cdk diff—to see what CloudFormation will change; this can catch many configuration errors before you deploy. If a cdk deploy fails, do not stop at the CDK output alone. Open the CloudFormation console for the corresponding stack and read the Events tab. Events present a chronological log of each resource action and will include status reasons for failures, such as missing permissions or invalid parameter values. Remember that the CDK command is a convenience: the runtime authority that maintains state and performs rollbacks is CloudFormation. This means your recovery steps involve CloudFormation actions like continue-update-rollback, manual resource deletion, or stack update once the root cause is corrected. A common misconception is to assume CDK will mask CloudFormation errors; it will not. Treat CDK as a template authoring layer and CloudFormation as the execution engine to debug.

CloudFormation’s automatic rollback is a safety net: if a stack creation or update fails, CloudFormation attempts to revert the stack to the previous stable state so you don’t end up with partially applied infrastructure. This behavior prevents inconsistent systems but does not remove the need for operator understanding. Rollbacks can fail, producing a ROLLBACK_FAILED state when CloudFormation cannot revert one or more resources. Typical reasons include manual modifications that introduced drift, custom resource delete handlers that return errors, or dependencies that block deletion. When that happens you must intervene: examine the Events log to identify the failing resource, inspect resource-specific logs such as CloudWatch Logs for custom Lambdas, and decide whether to manually revert the resource, delete it, or skip its rollback and continue using CloudFormation’s CLI options to target resources to skip. A common mistake is to immediately delete the stack when ROLLBACK_FAILED appears. Deleting the stack without understanding the retention policies can lead to data loss. Instead, identify the resource at fault, correct the underlying issue or use targeted operations to reach a stable state, and then re-run the update or delete. The best practice is to have DeletionPolicy configured for critical resources so a failed rollback does not result in unexpected data removal.

The primary troubleshooting tool for a failing CloudFormation deployment is the Events tab on the stack. Events present a chronological record of each action CloudFormation attempted and its outcome, including resource logical ID, action type, status, and a status reason when an error occurs. When you see a FAILED event, read the provided status reason: it commonly identifies an access-denied problem, an invalid parameter, or a resource creation failure. For custom resources the status reason may point to the custom Lambda failing; in that case, switch to the Lambda’s CloudWatch Logs. When diagnosing, take a methodical approach: first identify the earliest FAILED event in the timeline, then follow any dependent resource failures that cascade after that. Don’t assume the last event is the root cause. Also check whether the stack ended in ROLLBACK_COMPLETE or ROLLBACK_FAILED. If ROLLBACK_FAILED appears, the Events will tell you which resource could not be reverted, which is the place to start manual recovery. A misconception is to rely solely on the top-level CLI error; often the Events contain the precise resource-level detail you need to fix the problem. Use Events, then resource logs, then configuration or IAM fixes to resolve the root cause.

Custom resources extend CloudFormation with logic you implement, commonly in Lambda functions. Because CloudFormation may call create, update, and delete handlers multiple times, your handlers must be idempotent: running them more than once should result in the same end state as running them once. Implement idempotency by detecting existing resources or using stable identifiers so repeated calls do not create duplicates. For error handling, ensure your function catches exceptions and sends a clear FAILED signal back to CloudFormation with a helpful status reason. Logs are critical: if a custom resource fails, the Lambda’s CloudWatch Logs will contain stack traces and contextual details. A common error is missing try-except blocks or failing to handle timeout conditions, which prevents CloudFormation from receiving a proper failure response and can lead to rollback problems. Remember that CloudFormation will attempt to delete a resource during rollback; ensure your delete handler can handle partial state or missing dependencies gracefully. Treat custom resource development like A P I design: provide clear failure messages, handle retries safely, and document the expected lifecycle so debugging is straightforward when an error appears in Events.

DeletionPolicy is an attribute you apply to individual CloudFormation resources to control their behavior when the stack is deleted. There are three common values: Retain, Snapshot, and Delete. Retain ensures the resource persists after the stack is removed, which is useful for S3 buckets that contain critical data you cannot lose. Snapshot is appropriate for resources like RDS databases or EBS volumes where you want CloudFormation to create a final snapshot before deleting; that snapshot provides a recovery point. Delete is the default and allows CloudFormation to remove the resource during stack deletion. Applying DeletionPolicy is a safety decision: for production databases you usually want Snapshot, and for critical storage you often want Retain. A frequent operational error is omitting these settings and later discovering that a delete removed important data. The chapter provides a YAML snippet that shows how to set DeletionPolicy for a resource. Use these attributes thoughtfully and document the rationale in your templates so reviewers understand why a resource is being retained or snapshotted. Resource DeletionPolicy: Retain, Snapshot, Delete means set deletionpolicy to retain or snapshot for critical resources to prevent accidental data loss during stack deletion.. In practical terms, control what happens to resources when stacks are deleted. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Stack Termination Protection is a stack-level safeguard that prevents accidental deletion of an entire stack. When enabled, attempts to delete the stack will fail until termination protection is explicitly disabled. This is particularly important for production stacks that own critical resources. You can toggle termination protection in the console or via the CLI. Idempotency and permission hygiene are two pillars of safe IaC operations. Idempotency ensures that running the same operation multiple times yields the same result; this is especially important for custom resources and deployment scripts that may be retried during rollbacks. Implement idempotency by checking for existing resources, using stable names or identifiers, and writing delete handlers that tolerate partially created state. On the permission side, grant the deployment role only the actions required to provision the resources. Over-permissive roles can cause unintended changes or obscure failure causes. A common error is giving the role broad admin rights to avoid permission errors during testing, which hides the real permissions the template needs and increases blast radius in production. When you face an Access Denied status in Events, tighten the role by adding the minimal missing permissions rather than making the role overly permissive. Together, these practices reduce surprises during updates and make rollbacks and recovery steps more predictable and safe for production environments. When a deployment fails, a few error reasons appear repeatedly and each has a clear remediation path. Resource creation failed often points to misconfigured properties — compare the template properties against the resource documentation and correct invalid values such as wrong AMI IDs or invalid CIDR blocks. Access Denied indicates missing IAM permissions for the deployment role; identify the missing action in the Events and add the minimal permission rather than broadening the role excessively. Invalid parameter value means a parameter passed to the template is out of range or wrong type; validate parameter constraints and defaults and restrict allowed values where possible. Custom resource failures require inspecting the custom Lambda’s CloudWatch Logs to find exception traces, then making handlers idempotent and returning clear failure reasons. A practical remediation workflow is: 1) find the earliest FAILED event in Events, 2) read the status reason, 3) check resource logs if custom, 4) fix the template or permissions, and 5) redeploy. Avoid the trap of treating the last event as root cause — dependencies can cause cascading failures after the initial error. If rollback fails, plan manual remediation for the problematic resource and use the CLI to skip resources during continue-update-rollback only if you understand the consequences.

These are the essential concepts you should carry forward. First, CloudFormation is declarative and holds an internal stack state; use CloudFormation as the single source of truth for resources it manages. Second, automatic rollback protects stacks but can itself fail; when you see ROLLBACK_FAILED, diagnose the failing resource via Events and logs before deleting or recreating stacks. Third, protect critical data with DeletionPolicy settings and guard whole stacks with termination protection, and design custom resources to be idempotent and well-logged so failures are clear and recoverable. Keep these practices in mind as operational habits: check Events first, make handlers idempotent, and apply retention policies to avoid accidental data loss.
